opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck right now is really data, and specifically the right kind of data. If you look at what made AlphaFold possible, it was decades of painstakingly collected structures in the Protein Data Bank. That's a fantastic resource, but it's fairly static: it tells you what a protein looks like in one snapshot, usually in a crystal, not how it moves, how it behaves in a cell, or how strongly it binds to a partner.

When you move to protein–protein interactions or protein–small molecule binding, the data gets much sparser and much noisier. Binding affinity measurements come from many different labs using different assays and conditions, so the numbers often aren't directly comparable. There's also a strong publication bias. People tend to report the molecules that worked, so we have relatively few high-quality negative examples. For a model that's trying to learn what doesn't bind or what's toxic, that matters a lot.

So I'd say the limitation is less about model architecture. The transformer and diffusion-style models are quite expressive. It's more about having large-scale, standardized, functional data that captures dynamics, context, and the outcomes we actually care about, like efficacy and safety. That's why I'm excited about closing the loop between AI and experiments: using models to propose candidates, running high-throughput experiments, and feeding those results back in. Increasingly, AI agents can help design and interpret those experiments. If we can generate data purposefully, rather than relying on whatever happened to be published, I think that's where the next big jump will come from.

r001.rationale: The response calls data the biggest bottleneck and says progress depends on large-scale, standardized, functional data, clearly identifying data availability as the limiting factor.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest limitation, honestly, is data — but not in the simple sense of "we need more of it." It's the kind of data we have and how it's distributed.

If you look at what made AlphaFold possible, it was decades of structural biologists depositing hundreds of thousands of experimentally solved structures into the PDB. That was an extraordinary, well-curated public resource, and the model essentially learned to interpolate across it. But that same success also shows you the ceiling: the moment you move to protein-protein interactions, or protein-ligand complexes, or small molecule binding affinities, the amount of high-quality, consistently measured data drops by orders of magnitude. For interactions and binding, we have maybe tens of thousands of good examples rather than hundreds of thousands, and they're heavily biased toward a few well-studied protein families — kinases, GPCRs, things pharma has cared about historically. So the models look good on benchmarks that resemble the training distribution and then fall apart when you ask about a novel target or a chemotype that's genuinely new.

The second piece is that a lot of the data is noisy and inconsistent in ways that are hard to see. Binding assays from different labs use different conditions, different readouts, different definitions of what counts as a hit. When you pool that together, you're asking the model to learn a signal that's partly real biology and partly experimental artifact. In language and vision, scale washes that out. In biology, we don't have the scale to wash it out, so the noise matters a lot more.

And then the third thing, which I think gets underappreciated, is that the data we have is mostly static snapshots. Structures are crystal or cryo-EM snapshots; proteins in cells are dynamic, they have conformational ensembles, they're in crowded environments with post-translational modifications. Most of what determines whether a drug actually works — does it get to the right place, does it have off-target effects, is it tolerated — isn't captured in a static structure at all.

So when people ask whether we're going to get an "AlphaFold moment" for drug discovery, my answer is that the bottleneck isn't really the architecture or compute. It's that we need to generate data in a much more systematic way — ideally with the model in the loop, choosing which experiments to run so that each new data point is actually informative rather than another kinase inhibitor measurement. That's where I think a lot of the interesting work is right now: closing the loop between prediction and experiment, rather than just training bigger models on the data we happen to have.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the limited availability and quality of data for protein interactions and small-molecule binding as the main bottleneck, and explicitly says compute is not the primary limitation.

astra-6.text:
I think the main limitation is the data, especially high-quality experimental data. We have a lot of protein sequences, but knowing a sequence is very different from knowing what that protein does, what it interacts with, or how a small molecule will affect it in a cell.

And the data we do have are quite biased. We tend to study particular proteins and particular classes of molecules, and successful experiments are much more likely to be reported than experiments that didn’t work. That makes it difficult for a model to learn where the boundaries are and to generalize to something truly new.

So I think a big opportunity is to connect these models more closely with experiments: have the model suggest what would be useful to test, run those experiments, and feed the results back into the model, including the failures. Improving that feedback loop could be just as important as improving the model architecture.

r001.rationale: The response names data—especially high-quality experimental data—as the main limitation, distinguishing the abundance of sequences from the scarcity of functional and interaction information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main limitation is the data, especially high-quality experimental data. We have a lot of protein sequences, but for most of those proteins, we don’t know very much about what they actually do, what they interact with, or how those interactions change in different biological contexts. And for small molecules, the space of possible compounds is enormous compared with the tiny fraction that we’ve measured experimentally.

The data we do have are also biased toward the proteins and molecules that people have already chosen to study. So a model can do well on a benchmark but still struggle when you ask it to predict something genuinely different. I think a key opportunity is to connect these models more closely with experiments: use the model to propose informative experiments, measure the results, and then use those results to improve the model.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly names data, especially high-quality experimental data, as the main limitation and explains gaps in protein and small-molecule measurements.
